name: Kodungallur Kurumba Bhagavathy Temple
deity: Bhadrakali, worshipped here as Kurumba Bhagavathy or Kurumba Amma, the fierce and protective Mother of Kodungallur.
period: Chera-era tradition; one of the oldest Devi temples of Kerala, in its present medieval form
dynasty: Associated by tradition with the Chera country of the ancient Muziris coast
summary: Kodungallur Kurumba Bhagavathy Temple is among the oldest Devi shrines of Kerala, where Bhadrakali is worshipped as the Mother of the old port of Muziris and honoured in the great Bharani festival.

sections.history: Kodungallur is the ancient port usually identified with Muziris, where ships from Rome, Arabia and China once came to trade, and its Bhagavathy temple is counted among the oldest in Kerala. Its origins are told in more than one tradition. One credits Parasurama with installing the goddess; another links the shrine with the Chera king Chenkuttuvan and the cult of Kannaki, a connection that historians treat with caution. The temple is regarded as the head of the sixty-four Bhadrakali kavus, the goddess shrines of the Malabar region, and so holds a place of unusual honour in the devotional map of Kerala. Its present form belongs to the medieval period. Worshippers of many communities have long gathered here, and the temple is remembered as a place where the doors were open to all during the Bharani festival.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the traditional Kerala manner, a walled complex of sloping tiled roofs, timber work and lamp-lined courts around the srikovil. The sanctum of the goddess faces north, and she is worshipped in her ugra, or fierce, aspect. Within the complex a shrine of Shiva faces east, so that the Mother and her consort are honoured together. The outer enclosure, wide courtyard and old trees give the precinct a spacious, shaded quality, in keeping with the kavu tradition of goddess groves. Rather than ornament, the temple draws its force from its antiquity and from the steady rhythm of ritual around the sanctum.
sections.legends: The goddess of Kodungallur is Bhadrakali, the fierce form of the Mother who protects her devotees and removes affliction. Devotees tell of Parasurama, the sage who is said to have reclaimed the land of Kerala from the sea, installing her here to guard the country. A second tradition, found in Tamil literature, links the place with Kannaki, the heroine of the epic Silappatikaram, and with the Chera ruler Chenkuttuvan, though historians dispute that identification. Whatever the origin, the Mother is approached here with a mixture of awe and tenderness, as one who is both fearsome and close to her children.
sections.festivals: The great observance is the Bharani festival, which begins on the Bharani asterism in the Malayalam month of Kumbham, around March and April, and continues for about a week into Meenam. Its customs are unlike those of most temples: oracles known as velichappadus move around the shrine in the rite called Kavu Theendal, and pilgrims sing the ritual Bharani songs, with an old tradition of earthy, candid invocation of the goddess. Animal sacrifice, once part of the rites, is now prohibited by law. Thalappoli is another notable occasion; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Approach the temple with reverence and an unhurried mind. Outside the festival season the shrine is calm, shaded and quietly busy with local worshippers, and its sense of age is felt more than seen. During Bharani the town fills with pilgrims, music and fervour, and visitors should expect dense crowds and strong customs of their own. Kodungallur also rewards a wider visit, as the old Muziris coast holds some of the earliest layers of Kerala history, and the temple pairs naturally with other shrines of the circuit.

visit.timings: The temple generally opens in the early morning and again in the evening, with a midday closure, as is the custom in Kerala. Hours change during festivals, so please confirm timings locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Traditional attire is expected. Men are often asked to remove upper garments and wear a mundu, and women to dress modestly in a saree or similar. Please confirm the current requirements at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is typically not permitted near the sanctum and may be restricted in the precincts. Please ask staff and follow their instructions, especially during festivals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is in Kodungallur, Thrissur district, on the coast road between Thrissur and Ernakulam. The nearest railheads are at Thrissur and Ernakulam, and the nearest airport is Kochi. Kodungallur is well connected by road.
